content.text: Lethira chose the western signal stone because no living ranger had used it in six years.

It stood beyond the restored runestone line where Eversong’s enchanted spring gave way to the long sickness of the Ghostlands. White bark had grayed there. The grass lay in damp mats beneath thorn and ash, and the Dead Scar cut the eastern horizon with a darkness that morning could not soften. Falanaras waited ten paces behind Lethira with four Blood Knights and orders not to cross her line unless the meeting failed.

She had tied three strips of faded blue cloth to the stone. Ranger colors from before the fall, before crimson became grief worn as statecraft. The message was older than either of them: parley requested, familiar eyes preferred, approach from the south.
“If she does not come?” Falanaras asked.
Lethira kept her bow lowered. “Then I have spent half a night decorating a rock for the benefit of ghouls.”

The answer carried less bite than usual. She had opposed sending a written message through the field signals. Too many dark rangers had once read Thalassian hands, and too many of those hands now answered Sylvanas. So Lethira had come herself, carrying Halduron’s authority and Lor’themar’s request beneath a cloak whose hem had collected the Ghostlands mud.

Black-fletched arrows appeared first. Three points emerged between the trees, already fixed on gaps in Blood Knight armor. Serenya Duskrunner stepped into view after them. Rot had spared the precision of her movements. Her face remained the gray likeness of the ranger Lethira had known, emptied of warmth and sharpened by preservation spells. Five Forsaken followed in dark leathers, silent enough that the wet ground seemed to reject their weight.
Serenya looked at the blue cloth. “You remembered.”
“I remember many things I would prefer to forget.” Lethira’s gaze moved across the undead rangers and returned to Serenya. “Silvermoon requires a formal channel to your command.”
“To my command, or to my queen?”
Lethira’s fingers tightened around the bow grip. “To Sylvanas Windrunner.”

The old title went unspoken. Falanaras felt its absence among the trees. Ranger-General had once meant the shield of Quel’Thalas, a living certainty in blue and silver standing against the southern road. Banshee Queen meant a throne beneath another ruined kingdom. Both names belonged to the same woman. Neither could contain what Arthas had made between them.
Serenya studied Lethira for a long moment. “My queen expected this after your prince was disowned.”
“He was not disowned,” Falanaras said. “His authority was severed.”
Serenya’s dead eyes shifted to him. “The distinction may comfort the living.”

Lethira stepped between the exchange before pride could make policy more difficult. “We need scouts in the Ghostlands, pressure against Deatholme, and a route to powers beyond the Eastern Kingdoms that do not answer the Alliance. Your people need a northern force strong enough to keep the Scourge from rebuilding behind you. We have already proved those needs can share a battlefield.”
“Once,” Serenya said. “For less than an hour.”
“It was a productive hour.”

Something almost familiar passed across Serenya’s mouth and vanished. “My queen will send a delegation into Silvermoon to hear the request under your laws. If your city can endure that, she will receive Lor’themar at Windrunner Spire.”
Lethira looked west, toward ruins hidden beyond leagues of blight. “Her family’s home.”

“Her ground,” Serenya corrected. “She will not enter your living city to be displayed beneath guard. Your regent will not be asked to descend into hers before terms exist. The Spire belongs to memory and no present government. That is as close to neutral as our people are likely to find.”
Lethira untied one strip of blue cloth and held it out. Serenya accepted it with fingers that had once fletched arrows beside hers. Their hands did not touch.
Silvermoon endured the Forsaken poorly.

Serenya entered through the southern gate two mornings later with one deathguard and a hooded apothecary. Falanaras commanded the escort. Blood Knights surrounded the visitors in black plate, while magisters carried active ward-rods behind them and Farstriders watched the roofs. The precautions made the delegation resemble prisoners even though every order named them envoys.

Citizens withdrew from the avenue before the procession reached them. Shopkeepers pulled children indoors. A mana vendor abandoned an open tray of charged slivers rather than remain beside it as the undead passed. The shards shone unattended in green and violet rows, bright enough that three hungry onlookers stared at them despite the deathguard’s exposed jaw and the apothecary’s chemical stink.

An elderly ranger stood rigid beneath a restored arch. The left side of his face had been burned during the fall. When he recognized Serenya’s leathers, he raised two fingers in the old field salute before horror caught up with memory. His hand dropped. Serenya continued as though she had seen neither gesture.
Liadrin waited in the annex court with no helmet and both gauntlets fastened. Gold moved under her green eyes. The stolen Light had answered her anger before she permitted any of it into her hands.
“You will surrender weapons inside the council level,” she said.

Serenya unstrung her bow and gave it to Falanaras. The deathguard yielded a sword broad enough to split a shield. The apothecary produced six knives, two glass needles, a bone saw, and a stoppered vial that made the receiving magister’s ward-rod hiss.
“Medicinal,” the apothecary rasped.
“For whom?” Theron Brightshield asked from beside the doors.
The apothecary’s ruined lips parted. “That depends upon the dosage.”
Theron glanced at Falanaras. “Diplomacy already offers educational rewards.”
Liadrin did not share the humor. “Do not mistake entry for welcome,” she told Serenya. “Your freedom from the Lich King does not restore the lives the Scourge used your bodies to take.”
“No,” Serenya said. “Nor does your hatred restore mine.”

For an instant Falanaras thought Liadrin would end the meeting in the court. M’uru’s anguish stirred through him as her power rose nearby, a distant chime dragged through pain. Then she closed her hands. The radiance under her skin receded.
“The council is waiting,” she said.

Halduron had covered the table with casualty ledgers. Patrol losses in the Ghostlands stood beside maps of breaches along the runestone boundary and reports of Amani movement east of the Dead Scar. Black marks showed Scourge concentrations that had survived every limited strike. Each time the rangers destroyed one focus, two more appeared beyond roads they lacked the soldiers to hold.

Rommath’s contribution occupied less space and carried the same verdict. Reserve estimates had fallen again. The relay changes after Kael’thas’s severance consumed power faster than planned, civil wards strained under increased use, and M’uru’s public distribution conduits still failed whenever they extended beyond tightly governed chambers. Blood Knights relieved pressure on military supplies, but fourteen founders and a small number of later candidates could not feed a city one recipient at a time.
Lor’themar let Serenya read the table before he spoke. “Your queen offers aid.”
“She offers a hearing,” Serenya replied. “Aid follows terms.”
Rommath’s mouth tightened. “Then state the price of the hearing.”

“The Regent Lord travels to Windrunner Spire with a delegation small enough to prove he expects negotiation rather than battle. My queen will discuss patrol coordination, support against the Scourge, and sponsorship before the Horde. Nothing is promised beyond her advocacy. Thrall does not admit nations because Sylvanas Windrunner commands it.”
Liadrin stood over the map. “And if the Horde refuses?”
“Then you will still know what our aid costs.”

The council dismissed the Forsaken to guarded chambers and continued without them. No one argued that the old Horde had been harmless. Orcs and Amani had burned the border forests within living memory, and veterans still carried wounds from that war. The current Horde included trolls whose kin claimed Quel’Thalas as stolen land and undead who wore the faces of murdered defenders. Revulsion required no exaggeration to justify itself.

Halduron placed three casualty rolls beside the southern boundary. “Pride will not hold this line. Another incursion on the scale of the last breach will force us to strip the city wards or abandon villages. If the Amani strike at the same time, we lose both choices.”

“The Alliance will not come,” Rommath said. “Dalaran will not commit itself. The Argent Dawn will fight the Scourge beside us and refuse every obligation beyond the battlefield. Shattrath is separated from us by a demon-held road. These are the powers available, not the powers we would prefer.”
Liadrin stared at the marker representing Windrunner Spire. “Sylvanas once promised no enemy would enter these lands.”
“She died keeping that promise as long as anyone could,” Halduron said.
“And returned as the thing that entered.”
Lor’themar looked toward Falanaras, though the decision was not his to make. “You fought beside Serenya’s scouts.”

“They warned us of the breach, exposed the Scourge command line, and pulled our wounded clear,” Falanaras said. “They withdrew when Halduron ordered it. I would trust them to keep a field agreement whose purpose remains useful to them.”
“A narrow trust,” Liadrin said.
“It is wider than what Kael’thas left us.”

The words hurt more after he spoke them. Lor’themar gave no sign that pain altered their accuracy. He ordered Halduron to choose the route, Rommath to prepare terms concerning magical and military aid, and Liadrin to select a Blood Knight honor guard. Lethira would attend as the ranger who had opened the channel. Falanaras would command the guard.
When the meeting ended, Liadrin remained beside the casualty rolls. “We chain a being of Light beneath our city and recoil from corpses who broke their own chains.”
Falanaras waited.
“Do not mistake that for admiration,” she said. “I hate what they are. I hate that Arthas can still force their faces upon those who loved them. Yet hatred is a poor fortification.”
“It has held parts of this kingdom for years.”
“Then we have mistaken endurance for defense.” Liadrin lifted one of Halduron’s ledgers. “Choose six. We ride at dawn.”
They crossed the runestone boundary under a cold rain that turned the Ghostlands roads black.

Lor’themar rode beneath a plain crimson cloak with no royal device. Rommath traveled at his left, Liadrin at his right. Lethira and two Farstriders ranged ahead with Serenya’s scouts. Falanaras kept the six Blood Knights close enough to close around the delegation and far enough apart that a single necromantic strike could not take them all.

Nothing along the road pretended the Ghostlands had been reclaimed. Ruined farmsteads watched from behind dead orchards. Scourge marks appeared on stones the Farstriders had cleared a month earlier. Near a collapsed bridge, Serenya’s rangers found two ghouls crouched over a stag and killed them before the delegation came within bowshot. The bodies were dragged from the road. No banner rose over the work.

They kept west of Tranquillien. From a ridge, Falanaras saw the town’s broken roofs through the rain, empty except for drifting mist and movement that might have been Scourge. The road below could carry soldiers north or south. Whoever held it would place a hand around the throat of the Ghostlands. For now, no one did.

Windrunner Spire rose from the western blight near the sea, its towers broken and its pale stone stained by years without wards. One outer wall had fallen into a ravine. Dead ivy covered the surviving arch, and the Windrunner crest above it had been split through the center. The place retained the severe grace of a noble house built by rangers: narrow windows, high walks, open sightlines over every approach.

Forsaken archers occupied the walls without displaying a flag. Falanaras counted twenty before the gates opened and assumed he had missed half. Lethira counted too. Her mouth settled into the flat line she wore when memory threatened to become visible.
Sylvanas waited in the roofless great hall beneath a stair that led nowhere.

Falanaras had last seen her alive at a distance, bright armor moving along a failing defense while the Scourge pressed north. The figure before him carried the same poise after warmth, breath, and mercy had been cut away. Dark armor enclosed her narrow frame. A hood shadowed the gray severity of her face. Red eyes passed over the delegation, and the surviving hall seemed to contract around the attention.
“Lor’themar.” Her voice scraped softly against the stone. “You took your time.”
“Quel’Thalas spent years believing its prince would return.”
“Hope is most expensive when purchased in advance.” Sylvanas looked past him to Liadrin. “And now Silvermoon has discovered other forms of credit.”
Liadrin’s jaw tightened. “If you mean M’uru, name the captive.”
A colder interest entered Sylvanas’s expression. “So the rumors are modest. Good. The Horde will prefer an ugly truth it can measure.”
Lor’themar did not look at Liadrin. “We came to discuss the Ghostlands and your sponsorship.”

“They are the same discussion. Thrall will ask what you bring, what you require, and which disasters will follow you into his councils. Your hunger. Your fel use. Your prince’s treachery. Your captive Light.” Sylvanas moved to a cracked table where a map of the northern kingdoms had been pinned beneath knives. “I can make your usefulness louder than your liabilities. I cannot make either disappear.”
Rommath approached the map. “State what advocacy requires.”

“Silvermoon petitions as a nation prepared to join, not as a client seeking charity. If admitted, you answer Horde calls with soldiers, intelligence, and passage where your territory makes passage necessary. You coordinate with Forsaken forces against the Scourge from the Plaguelands to the runestone boundary. You do not use our dead as a convenient shield while reserving every victory for yourselves.”

Lor’themar placed one hand on the edge of the table. “No Forsaken garrison enters Eversong without invitation. No Horde force acquires land in Quel’Thalas through service. Tranquillien and the roads around it remain blood elf territory whether or not we presently hold them.”

“Territory unheld is a claim written for the benefit of maps.” Sylvanas’s nail rested over Tranquillien. “My scouts already bleed on those roads. They will continue using them. They will raise no banner and establish no permanent post until boundaries are agreed. In return, your rangers share signals, your commanders answer warnings, and your patrols stop treating every Forsaken movement as an invasion.”

Halduron had sent Lethira with authority over field practice. She stepped to the map. “Signals can be shared by assigned units. Joint operations require named commanders and defined objectives. Your scouts withdraw south of the boundary when the objective ends.”
Sylvanas regarded her. “Valeflame. You used to object less when I assigned a field.”

“I remember.” The words held no plea. Sylvanas’s gaze moved past Lethira to the broken stair, and for one breath the ruin held her attention without serving any argument. “I also remember dying because the southern approaches were too weak and help was too far away. I will not repeat the error to protect your comfort.”
“I remember.” The words held no plea. “I also remember dying because the southern approaches were too weak and help was too far away. I will not repeat the error to protect your comfort.”

The argument continued through patrol numbers, supply caches, courier rights, and the treatment of wounded taken by the other force. Every term exposed another place where trust was absent and cooperation might still function. Falanaras understood why Sylvanas had chosen a ruined home. No polished chamber could have held the conversation honestly. They were bargaining over how much of the wound each side could enter without claiming it.
At last Sylvanas turned toward the honor guard. “These are the soldiers built from your captive.”
“Blood Knights,” Liadrin said.
“Paladins without faith.”
“Soldiers with discipline.”
Sylvanas pointed to Falanaras. “Show me what that distinction buys.”

Liadrin gave the smallest nod. Falanaras drew a measured current. M’uru answered across the distance beneath Silvermoon. Pain entered first, vast and controlled by nothing except the restraints around the naaru and Falanaras’s choice of how much to take. Red-gold Light gathered over his gauntlet. He formed it into a compact barrier, turned the edge of a falling raindrop through the open roof, and ended the draw before warmth became appetite.
The dead rangers along the walls recoiled from the radiance. Sylvanas did not.
“How many?” she asked.

“Enough to have held southern Eversong when Serenya’s scouts brought warning,” Liadrin said. “Enough to heal wounded rangers, break Scourge workings, and destroy what crossed our boundary. Fewer than the Horde will want. More than our enemies expect.”
“And every use hurts the source.”
“Yes.”

Sylvanas looked from Liadrin to Lor’themar. “Thrall will despise the method. He may respect that you admit it. The orcs know what stolen power can make of a people.” Her red gaze returned to Falanaras. “Can your knight stop when victory is available?”
“He just did,” Liadrin said.
“In a hall, before his commander.” Sylvanas’s expression hardened with old military contempt. “The Horde will want proof under pressure.”
Falanaras met her gaze. “Then it should test me under pressure.”
The silence that followed carried the attention of every archer on the walls. Sylvanas inclined her head by the smallest degree, accepting an answer rather than granting approval.

By dusk they had a provisional understanding. Forsaken scouts could continue operating along the Ghostlands roads without territorial claim. Assigned ranger units would share warnings and coordinate limited actions against the Scourge. No force would cross the restored boundary in strength without invitation except to pursue an immediate threat. Silvermoon would petition for Horde membership and accept military obligations if admitted. Sylvanas would carry the petition before Thrall and the other leaders.
“You will come to Undercity,” Sylvanas said. “The Horde will judge you where it can see what I am risking on your behalf.”
Lor’themar fastened his seal beneath the terms. “And what are you risking?”

Rain moved across the dark sea beyond the broken western wall. Sylvanas watched it for a moment longer than the question required. “The chance that you will mistake survival for independence once more.”
Rumor reached Silvermoon before the delegation returned.

Someone had seen Forsaken envoys at the annex. Someone else knew Lor’themar had ridden south beneath guard. By the time Falanaras passed through the city gate, handbills accused the Regent Lord of selling the Ghostlands to Sylvanas, surrendering Silvermoon to orcs, and inviting Amani trolls to finish what the Scourge began. The details contradicted one another. Fear gave them a common authority.

The largest gathering filled the Walk of Elders near a dry reflecting pool. A priest in faded white and red stood on the rim, speaking to several hundred citizens. His robes belonged to the old clergy rather than Liadrin’s order. Hunger trembled in his hands, though his voice carried clearly across the square.

“The orcs came north with the Amani,” he called. “They burned our forests and called it conquest. The undead murdered our families and returned wearing them. Now we are told these are our protectors. We cast down one absent prince and kneel to a dead ranger in the same week.”

Agreement rolled through the crowd. Falanaras heard grief beneath it, and the sharper relief of people given enemies they already understood. Theron waited beside a patrol at the edge of the pool. When he saw Falanaras, he tipped his head toward the speaker.
“He has been careful,” Theron said. “No call to violence. No attempt to breach a ward. He tells history in the order most useful to his conclusion.”
“That remains legal.”
“At the moment.”

Three magisters entered the square from the eastern arcade. Between them walked another priest in formal crimson, his eyes fixed on the speaker with disciplined vacancy. The crowd quieted as the magisters raised restraint sigils. Theron’s patrol had received no order to advance. Falanaras realized the purpose of the second priest one breath before the spell reached the first.

Shadow gathered around the crimson-robed priest’s fingers and crossed the pool in a thin violet thread. The speaker stiffened. His mouth remained open while every muscle in his face fought a command no one else could hear. One magister sealed the square against interruption. Another laid an amplification charm over the captive voice.

“I have spoken from fear,” the priest said. His tone had become smooth and dead. “The Regent Lord seeks strength for Quel’Thalas. The Forsaken are free allies against the Scourge. The Horde offers honorable fellowship. Silvermoon must stand with those prepared to defend her.”

The crowd listened in horror. A woman near the front began reciting the words with him, perhaps from agreement, perhaps because agreement suddenly looked safer. Others followed. The coerced declaration spread unevenly through the square until several hundred voices praised an alliance no treaty had yet created.
Falanaras moved before deciding what intervention would mean. Theron caught his forearm.
“If you break the spell,” Theron said quietly, “the magisters arrest you beside him. Then the city learns the Blood Knights oppose the Regent Lord’s road.”
“Do we support this?”
“No.” Theron’s grip remained firm. “We support Quel’Thalas. You warned me that answer was doing a great deal of work.”
The controlled priest smiled. Tears ran down his face while his mouth proclaimed loyalty to the Horde.

Falanaras had seen bodies compelled in Deatholme. Necromantic strings had been cruder, tearing flesh when the dead resisted. The violence here left no wound for a healer to close. It entered memory, speech, and public record. By nightfall, officials would report that an anti-Horde gathering had dispersed after its leader withdrew his objections.
The spell ended. The priest collapsed into the reflecting pool. There was no water to soften the fall.
Liadrin received Falanaras’s report in M’uru’s outer vault.

The naaru’s captive radiance rose beyond layers of stone and restraint. Its presence pressed against every Blood Knight in the chamber, offering relief entwined with pain. Liadrin stood beneath it while attendants fitted travel seals to her armor. On a nearby table lay the provisional terms from Windrunner Spire and the formal summons to Undercity.
“A vow spoken through another person’s mouth has no worth,” she said when he finished.
“The magisters called it correction of incitement.”

“Of course they did.” Liadrin dismissed the attendants. When the doors shut, anger entered her voice. “I will stand before orcs, trolls, and the undead and argue that this alliance may preserve our people. I will not pretend the people already consent.”
“Will you challenge the order?”

“Lor’themar did not issue that method. He has declined to revoke the emergency authority that permits it.” She looked toward M’uru. “We have become skilled at placing distance between a decision and the suffering that serves it.”

M’uru’s pain moved through Falanaras in a low sustained pulse. Above them, the city prepared proclamations describing fellowship and mutual defense. Below, a captive supplied the power of the soldiers who would embody that argument before the Horde.

Liadrin fastened the last clasp on her gauntlet. “You will travel with me. Rommath comes to answer for our magic. Lethira comes because Sylvanas listens to rangers who have bled in the same ground as hers. Lor’themar will speak for the kingdom. You will speak for the Blood Knights if the Horde asks what we are.”
“What answer do you want me to give?”

“The true one. We took power from a captive because it saved lives. We govern the taking because need does not govern itself. We are effective. We are dangerous. If they require innocence, we will return alone.”

At the barracks, Theron helped select the remaining honor guard. He did not ask to join. Someone had to hold the Blood Knight patrols inside a city where loyalty could now be placed in a citizen’s mouth by force. Lethira arrived with her travel bow, three spare strings, and an expression suggesting every available road had offended her personally.
“Windrunner Spire was insufficient?” Theron asked.
“Apparently we must now inspect the kingdom buried beneath Lordaeron.” Lethira set down her pack. “I had worried this alliance might become pleasant.”
Theron looked to Falanaras. “And after Undercity?”
“If they admit us, obligations. If they refuse, the same borders with fewer illusions.”
“A favorable range of outcomes.”

Outside, patrol bells marked curfew. Magisters moved through the lower streets beneath new notices forbidding agitation against recognized diplomatic envoys. Somewhere beyond the restored walls, Forsaken scouts watched roads Silvermoon could not hold. Farther south and west, the Horde waited to decide whether blood elves belonged among its old enemies and wounded peoples.

Falanaras secured his sword across his back and felt M’uru’s distant suffering beneath the familiar warmth in his chest. The power would travel with him into Undercity. So would the coerced priest’s tears, Kael’thas’s silence, Rynel’s final restraint, and the memory of Sylvanas standing inside the ruin of her own name.
Silvermoon had counted the monsters near enough to help. At dawn, it would go below the ruins of Lordaeron and ask to stand among them.
